# 6 Pragmatism as Mediator Between Empiricism and Religion

Pragmatism may be a happy harmonizer of empiricist ways of thinking, with the more religious demands of human beings.[^1]

Men who are strongly of the fact-loving temperament[^2] are liable to be kept at a distance by the small sympathy with facts which that philosophy from the present-day fashion of idealism offers them.[^3] It is far too intellectualistic.[^4] Old fashioned theism was bad enough, with its notion of God as an exalted monarch, made up of a lot of unintelligible or preposterous 'attributes'; but, so long as it held strongly by the argument from design, it kept some touch with concrete realities.[^5] Since, however, darwinism has once for all displaced design from the minds of the 'scientific,' theism has lost that foothold; and some kind of an immanent or pantheistic deity working IN things rather than above them is, if any, the kind recommended to our contemporary imagination.[^6] Aspirants to a philosophic religion turn, as a rule, more hopefully nowadays towards idealistic pantheism than towards the older dualistic theism, in spite of the fact that the latter still counts able defenders.[^7]

But,[^8] the brand of pantheism offered is hard for them to assimilate if they are lovers of facts, or empirically minded.[^9] It is the absolutistic brand, spurning the dust and reared upon pure logic.[^10] It keeps no connexion whatever with concreteness.[^11] Affirming the Absolute Mind, which is its substitute for God, to be the rational presupposition of all particulars of fact, whatever they may be, it remains supremely indifferent to what the particular facts in our world actually are.[^12] Be they what they may, the Absolute will father them.[^13] You cannot redescend into the world of particulars by the Absolute's aid, or deduce any necessary consequences of detail important for your life from your idea of his nature.[^14] He gives you indeed the assurance that all is well with Him, and for his eternal way of thinking; but thereupon he leaves you to be finitely saved by your own temporal devices.[^15]

But from the human point of view, no one can pretend that it doesn't suffer from the faults of remoteness and abstractness.[^16] It is eminently a product of[^17] the rationalistic temper.[^18] It disdains empiricism's needs.[^19] It substitutes a pallid outline for the real world's richness.[^20] It is dapper; it is noble in the bad sense, in the sense in which to be noble is to be inapt for humble service.[^21] In this real world of sweat and dirt,[^22] when a view of things is 'noble,' that ought to count as a presumption against its truth, and as a philosophic disqualification.[^23] The prince of darkness may be a gentleman, as we are told he is, but whatever the God of earth and heaven is, he can surely be no gentleman.[^24] His menial services are needed in the dust of our human trials, even more than his dignity is needed in the empyrean.[^25]

Now pragmatism, devoted tho she be to facts, has no such materialistic bias as ordinary empiricism labors under.[^26] Moreover, she has no objection whatever to the realizing of abstractions, so long as you get about among particulars with their aid and they actually carry you somewhere.[^27] Interested in no conclusions but those which our minds and our experiences work out together, she has no a priori prejudices against theology.[^28] IF THEOLOGICAL IDEAS PROVE TO HAVE A VALUE FOR CONCRETE LIFE, THEY WILL BE TRUE, FOR PRAGMATISM, IN THE SENSE OF BEING GOOD FOR SO MUCH.[^29] FOR HOW MUCH MORE THEY ARE TRUE, WILL DEPEND ENTIRELY ON THEIR RELATIONS TO THE OTHER TRUTHS THAT ALSO HAVE TO BE ACKNOWLEDGED.[^30]

What I, William James,[^31] said just now about the Absolute of transcendental idealism is a case in point.[^32] First, I called it majestic and said it yielded religious comfort to a class of minds, and then I accused it of remoteness and sterility.[^33] But so far as it affords such comfort, it surely is not sterile; it has that amount of value; it performs a concrete function.[^34] As a good pragmatist, I myself ought to call the Absolute true 'in so far forth,' then; and I unhesitatingly now do so.[^35]

But what does TRUE IN SO FAR FORTH mean in this case?[^36] To answer, we need only apply the pragmatic method.[^37] What do believers in the Absolute mean by saying that their belief affords them comfort?[^38] They mean that since in the Absolute finite evil is 'overruled' already, we may, therefore, whenever we wish, treat the temporal as if it were potentially the eternal, be sure that we can trust its outcome, and, without sin, dismiss our fear and drop the worry of our finite responsibility.[^39] In short, they mean that we have a right ever and anon to take a moral holiday, to let the world wag in its own way, feeling that its issues are in better hands than ours and are none of our business.[^40]

The universe is a system of which the individual members may relax their anxieties occasionally, in which the don't-care mood is also right for men, and moral holidays in order--that, if I mistake not, is part, at least, of what the Absolute is 'known-as,' that is the great difference in our particular experiences which his being true makes for us, that is part of his cash-value when he is pragmatically interpreted.[^41] Farther than that the ordinary lay-reader in philosophy who thinks favorably of absolute idealism does not venture to sharpen his conceptions.[^42] He can use the Absolute for so much, and so much is very precious.[^43] He is pained at hearing you speak incredulously of the Absolute, therefore, and disregards your criticisms because they deal with aspects of the conception that he fails to follow.[^44]

If the Absolute means this, and means no more than this, who can possibly deny the truth of it?[^45] To deny it would be to insist that men should never relax, and that holidays are never in order.[^46] I am well aware how odd it must seem to some of you to hear me say that an idea is 'true' so long as to believe it is profitable to our lives.[^47] That it is GOOD, for as much as it profits, you will gladly admit.[^48] If what we do by its aid is good, you will allow the idea itself to be good in so far forth, for we are the better for possessing it.[^49] But is it not a strange misuse of the word 'truth,' you will say, to call ideas also 'true' for this reason?[^50]
